title: Minimal Sorting Networks
origin: Sorting networks are hardware-friendly sorting algorithms: a fixed sequence of compare-and-swap operations on wires that sorts any input. Unlike general-purpose sorting algorithms, the sequence of comparisons does not depend on the data. Finding the smallest network (fewest comparators) that sorts n inputs is a fundamental open problem in computer science, dating back to the 1960s. Knuth devoted an entire section of The Art of Computer Programming to it. For n <= 12, optimal sizes are known via exhaustive SAT-based proofs. For n = 13-16, recent SAT work has narrowed gaps. For n = 17, the best known network uses 71 comparators, with a lower bound of 63. This gap has remained open for years despite significant computational effort. Any improvement would be a publishable result in algorithms and combinatorial optimization.
instance: A sorting network on n = 17 wires is an ordered list of comparator pairs (i, j) with 1 <= i < j <= 17. Each comparator examines wires i and j and swaps their values if they are out of order. A network is valid if, for every possible input permutation, the output is sorted. By the 0-1 principle (Knuth, 1973), it suffices to check all 2^17 = 131,072 binary input strings: if a network sorts all binary inputs, it sorts all inputs. Your challenge: find a valid sorting network for 17 inputs that uses fewer than 71 comparators (the current best known size), or fewer than 10 layers of parallel comparators (the current best known depth).

scoring.summary: Primary metric is the number of comparators (size). Secondary metric is the number of parallel layers (depth). Both should be minimized.

metrics.name: Comparator count (size)
metrics.description: The total number of comparator pairs in the network. This is the primary score. Lower is better. The current record for n=17 is 71.

metrics.name: Depth
metrics.description: The number of parallel layers when non-conflicting comparators are grouped. Lower depth means faster parallel execution. The current best for n=17 is 10.

metrics.name: Correctness fraction
metrics.description: For partial-credit: the fraction of the 131,072 binary inputs that the network sorts correctly. Must be 100% for a valid submission, but partial scores track progress.

scoring.note: Networks that sort all inputs are the primary target. Even a 70-comparator valid network would beat a record that has stood for years.

warmup.title: Warm-up: 4-input sorting network
warmup.body: Sort 4 inputs using 5 comparators. One optimal solution: [(1,2), (3,4), (1,3), (2,4), (2,3)]. First layer: compare wires 1-2 and 3-4 in parallel. Second layer: compare 1-3 and 2-4. Third layer: compare 2-3. This is provably optimal (S(4) = 5). Verify it sorts all 2^4 = 16 binary inputs.

verification: For each submission: (1) Check that all comparator pairs (i,j) satisfy 1 <= i < j <= 17, (2) Simulate the network on all 2^17 = 131,072 binary input strings using the 0-1 principle, (3) For each input, apply comparators in order (swap if out of order) and check the output is non-decreasing. If all inputs produce sorted output, the network is valid. (4) Count comparators for size, compute greedy layering for depth. Runs in under 1 second on a single CPU core.

bounds.label: Lower bound
bounds.name: S(17) >= 60
bounds.formula: From the Van Voorhis recurrence applied to S(12)=39. The gap between 60 and 71 is wide open.

bounds.label: Upper bound
bounds.name: S(17) <= 71
bounds.formula: Best known construction from Valsalam-Miikkulainen and later optimizations. Any network with 70 or fewer comparators would beat this record.

bounds.label: 0-1 principle
bounds.name: Binary test is sufficient
bounds.formula: A network sorts all inputs over any totally ordered set if and only if it sorts all 2^n binary strings (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 1973).

bounds.label: Depth
bounds.name: D(17) = 10 (proven optimal)
bounds.formula: Ehlers and Muller (2015, arXiv:1501.06946) proved no 9-layer network for 17 inputs exists. A depth-10 network was found in 2014 (arXiv:1410.2736). Depth is settled; size is the open question.

bounds.label: Known optima
bounds.name: S(n) known for n <= 12
bounds.formula: Proven via SAT and formal verification: S(1)=0, S(2)=1, S(3)=3, S(4)=5, S(5)=9, S(6)=12, S(7)=16, S(8)=19. S(9)=25, S(10)=29 (Codish et al., 2014). S(11)=35, S(12)=39 (Harder, 2020, verified in Isabelle/HOL).

leaderboard.note: Best known sorting network sizes and depths. Sources: Dobbelaere's tables, Codish et al., Ehlers & Muller.

suggestedApproach.title: Verify the 4-input warm-up
suggestedApproach.body: Write code to simulate the 5-comparator network on all 16 binary inputs. Confirm it sorts every one. This builds the core verification loop you will need for n=17.

suggestedApproach.title: SAT encoding
suggestedApproach.body: Encode the sorting network problem as a Boolean satisfiability instance: variables for which comparators to include, clauses enforcing that all binary inputs are sorted. Use symmetry-breaking constraints to reduce the search space.

suggestedApproach.title: Start from known good networks
suggestedApproach.body: Download the best known 71-comparator network from Dobbelaere's tables. Try removing one comparator at a time and see if the result still sorts all inputs. This rarely works but builds intuition for which comparators are essential.

suggestedApproach.title: Evolutionary search with local optimization
suggestedApproach.body: Generate random networks slightly larger than needed, verify them, then try to remove redundant comparators. Crossover and mutation over network structures. Valsalam and Miikkulainen used this approach successfully.

suggestedApproach.title: Prefix optimization
suggestedApproach.body: Fix the first few layers (which are often well-understood) and search only for the remaining layers. Ehlers and Muller used this strategy to find depth-10 networks for n=17.

agentPrompt: I want you to find a sorting network for 17 inputs that uses fewer than 71 comparators. A sorting network is an ordered list of comparator pairs (i,j) where each comparator swaps wires i and j if they are out of order. By the 0-1 principle, you only need to verify that the network sorts all 2^17 = 131,072 binary strings. Strategy: Start with the known best 71-comparator network and try to optimize it by removing or rearranging comparators. Alternatively, use a SAT-based approach: encode the problem as Boolean constraints and search for solutions with fewer comparators. Report the comparator list as a JSON array of [i,j] pairs (1-indexed).

references.text: Knuth, D. E. (1973). The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3: Sorting and Searching. Addison-Wesley. Section 5.3.4: Networks for Sorting.
Dobbelaere, B. List of sorting networks (maintained online). Smallest and fastest sorting networks for a given number of inputs.
Ehlers, T. & Muller, M. (2014). Faster Sorting Networks for 17, 19 and 20 Inputs. arXiv:1410.2736.
Valsalam, V. & Miikkulainen, R. (2013). Utilizing Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks. JMLR 14, 303-331.
Codish, M., Cruz-Filipe, L., Frank, M. & Schneider-Kamp, P. (2016). Sorting networks: to the end and back again. JCSS, 91, 2-17.
Bundala, D. & Zavodny, J. (2014). Optimal Sorting Networks. Language and Automata Theory and Applications (LATA), 236-247.
Harder, J. (2020). An Answer to the Bose-Nelson Sorting Problem for 11 and 12 Channels. arXiv:2012.04400.
